html:
The Quapaw, who call themselves O-ga-xpa, "downstream people", are a Dhegiha Siouan people of the lower Arkansas River, near where it joins the Mississippi. By their own history they once lived in the Ohio valley with the Osage, Omaha, Kaw and Ponca, and moved down the Mississippi while the others went up the Missouri. The French called them the Arkansas, which gave the state its name.

In 1673 Marquette and Jolliet ended their voyage down the Mississippi at Quapaw villages. In 1686 the French built Arkansas Post nearby, and the Quapaw became firm allies of French Louisiana. Smallpox in 1698 and later epidemics killed most of them.

After the Louisiana Purchase the United States took their land by treaties, and in the 1830s they were moved to the northeast corner of today's Oklahoma. Lead and zinc mining later poisoned their land there. See also the map's other Quapaw territory.
